lead: A plane truss is straight members joined at pins. If members plus reaction components equal twice the joints, joint equilibrium alone finds every force. If they are more, extra members are redundant: equilibrium leaves their forces free, and compatibility of deformation must supply one equation per redundant. Trusses appear in engine mounts, landing-gear bays and older wing ribs. The count decides what is solvable; the method of joints does the solving.
prereq: You need: equilibrium of concurrent forces and free body diagrams; the axial strain energy P²L/(2AE) from strain energy is used for the redundant truss.

blocks.text: Use a plane truss. Let m be members, r independent reaction components, j joints. Each pin joint gives ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, so 2j equations. Unknowns: m member forces plus r reactions. The count is below.

blocks.where: m members; r reactions; j joints; D degree.

blocks.text: D = 0 means determinate: equilibrium gives every force. D > 0 means indeterminate to degree D: D extra equations are needed, one compatibility condition per redundant. D < 0 means a mechanism: the truss cannot carry general load. Count supports as pin r = 2 and roller r = 1. A fixed support has r = 3 but is rare in a plane truss. A roof truss with m = 7, r = 3, j = 5 has D = 7 + 3 − 10 = 0. This count is done before any force is calculated. It is necessary but not enough: the members must also be arranged so that no part can move. Two members that cross without a pin, or three reactions that are all parallel or all meet at one point, can give D = 0 and still leave a mechanism, so check the arrangement as well as the count.

The method rests on the ideal truss: straight members joined by frictionless pins, loads applied only at the joints, and self-weight neglected or lumped at the joints. Each member is then a two-force member that carries pure tension or compression along its own axis. A member loaded between its joints also bends and needs beam analysis.
Assume tension positive: member force pulls its joint away. Negative is compression. Begin where at most two member forces are unknown.

items: Find reactions from the whole truss as one free body.
Choose a joint with at most two unknown member forces.
Draw the joint alone. Replace each cut member by its force, arrow away for tension.
Write ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. Solve the two equations.
Move to the next joint. Carry every solved force with its sign.
Repeat until all member forces are found.

blocks.text: At an unloaded joint, two non-collinear members carry zero force. Three members with two collinear leave the third zero. Inspection works only when no external load or support reaction acts at that joint. The method gives forces, not deflections; deflections come from the unit load method.

If D > 0, one compatibility condition per redundant is needed. Remove a redundant, find the gap, close it; Section 3 does this for a three-bar truss. The method alone cannot start every joint in a redundant truss.

sections.h3: One redundant member: least work and checking a computer result

blocks.text: Call the force in the redundant member X. Cut it, and the truss left is determinate. Every member force is then N = N₀ + Xn, where N₀ comes from the real loads on the cut truss and n from a pair of unit pulls at the cut.
U = Σ N²L/(2AE)        ∂U/∂X = Σ N n L/(AE) = 0
blocks.where: U is the strain energy of all members including the redundant one; X is the redundant force; n is ∂N/∂X. The zero says the two faces of the cut do not separate.

items: Write N = N₀ + Xn for every member, the redundant itself having N = X and n = 1.
Set Σ (N₀ + Xn) n L/(AE) = 0 and solve for X.
Any member may be chosen as the redundant; the final forces are the same, only the arithmetic changes.

blocks.text: A matrix program gives every force and deflection at once. Check it by hand before trusting it: equilibrium at two or three joints, one member force by the method of joints, and one deflection by the unit load method. A small error in a support condition shows up at once in these checks.

Right: three bars from a ceiling meeting at D, the middle bar vertical and the outer bars at 45 degrees, 50 kilonewtons hanging from D, middle bar labelled X equals 29.29 and outer bars 14.64.

examples.question: A triangular truss has pin A and roller B on the same level, 4 m apart. Apex C is 2 m above midspan. A vertical load of 10 kN acts downward at C. Find the degree of indeterminacy and all member forces by the method of joints. Use tension positive.
steps: m = 3, r = 3 (pin 2, roller 1), j = 3; D = 3 + 3 − 6 = 0, and the triangle cannot fold, so the truss is determinate.
Whole truss: ΣFy gives Ay + By = 10 kN. Symmetry gives Ay = By = 5 kN.
Let θ be the angle each rafter makes with the bottom chord AB. Rafter AC rises 2 m over 2 m, length √(2² + 2²) = 2.828 m, so sin θ = cos θ = 2/2.828 = 0.7071.
Joint A, vertical, tension positive: 5 kN + AC × 0.7071 = 0, so AC = −7.07 kN, compression.
Joint A, horizontal: AB + (−7.07 kN × 0.7071) = 0, so AB = +5.00 kN, tension.
Check at C: the two rafters push up with 2 × 7.07 kN × 0.7071 = 10 kN, balancing the load.
examples.answer: D = 0; AB = +5.00 kN tension, AC = BC = −7.07 kN (7.07 kN compression each).

examples.question: Three aluminium bars meet at a pin D and hang it from a rigid frame. The middle bar is vertical and 2 m long; the outer bars are at 45° to it on either side, so each is 2√2 = 2.828 m long. All bars have A = 300 mm² and E = 70 GPa. A load P = 50 kN hangs from D. Find the force in each bar and the deflection of D.
steps: Count: m = 3, j = 4 (D and three frame pins), r = 6 (two at each frame pin). D = 3 + 6 − 8 = 1, so one bar is redundant. Choose the middle bar, force X.
Cut truss: the two outer bars carry P alone. Vertical equilibrium at D: 2F cos 45° = P − X, so F = (P − X)/√2 in each outer bar.
Outer bars: F = X/2 = 14.64 kN each. Check at D: 29.29 + 2 × 14.64 × 0.7071 = 50.0 kN.
Stresses: 29 290/300 = 97.6 MPa in the middle bar, 48.8 MPa in each outer bar.
AE = 300 × 10⁻⁶ × 70 × 10⁹ = 2.1 × 10⁷ N. Deflection of D = stretch of the middle bar = 29 290 × 2/(2.1 × 10⁷) = 2.79 × 10⁻³ m = 2.79 mm.
Compatibility check: each outer bar stretches 14 645 × 2.828/(2.1 × 10⁷) = 1.97 mm = 2.79 × cos 45°, the component of D’s movement along it.
examples.answer: Middle bar 29.29 kN, each outer bar 14.64 kN, all in tension; D moves 2.79 mm down. Without the middle bar the outer bars would carry 35.36 kN each and D would drop 6.73 mm.

traps: Counting a roller as two reactions; pin r = 2, roller r = 1.
Calling D > 0 unsolvable; it asks for one compatibility condition per redundant.
Reversing tension: tension pulls away from the joint, so a negative result is compression.
Starting at a joint with three or more unknowns and getting stuck.
Removing a zero-force member from the design; it may matter in another load case.

quiz.q: Define m, r, j and D for a plane truss.
quiz.a: m members, r reaction components, j joints; D = m + r − 2j.
Equilibrium leaves D redundants; compatibility supplies D extra equations.

quiz.q: A truss has m = 9, r = 4, j = 6. Find D.
At an unloaded joint, two non-collinear members meet. Prove both forces are zero.
quiz.a: ΣFx and ΣFy give two equations; the only solution is both zero.

quiz.q: Same triangular truss has 20 kN at C. Find Ay and AC.
Why start at a joint with at most two unknowns?
quiz.a: Two equilibrium equations solve at most two unknown forces.

quiz.q: At an unloaded joint, three members meet, two collinear. What is the third force?
quiz.a: Zero; resolving perpendicular to the collinear pair leaves only the third force.

quiz.q: In worked example 2 the middle bar takes 59 % of the load. Why does it take more than either outer bar?
quiz.a: All three bars must fit the same movement of D. The middle bar is shorter (2 m against 2.83 m) and lies along the load, so it stretches by the full deflection; each outer bar stretches only Δcos 45° over a longer length. Its strain is twice theirs, so its stress and force are twice theirs: X = 2F.

beyond: Not for the exam. Truss analysis feeds finite element programs: each member becomes a two-force spring with a stiffness matrix. Redundant trusses are solved by the same compatibility idea, often with matrix methods. Aircraft engine mounts and landing gear still use determinate trusses for easy inspection. Search next for 'truss finite element stiffness matrix' and 'redundant truss compatibility'.
